name: Brow growth serum
lead: Brow growth serums are cosmetic products marketed to make eyebrows look thicker or longer. Many are peptide- or botanical-based; Wikipedia notes that some lash-growth brands use peptides rather than prostaglandins because of regulations in Canada and California.[1]

Published evidence is sparse. A manufacturer-sponsored 2024 safety study tested a lash and brow serum for skin irritation rather than for growth,[2] and a small registered trial of a brow serum is listed as completed, with no results located.[3]
infobox: Cosmetic claims; prostaglandin products restricted in some jurisdictions

paras: Cosmetic lash and brow conditioners using seed extracts, minerals and peptides have grown in popularity over the past decade.[1] They are distinct from prostaglandin-analog products: bimatoprost (Latisse) was introduced in 2009 as the first FDA-approved eyelash growth treatment, with noticeable growth over about 16 weeks.[1] A published case report described eyebrow thickening in one woman treated with bimatoprost 0.03 percent over eight months, which is a single case rather than a controlled trial.[4]

Cosmetics applied near the eye can cause skin sensitivity reactions, and manufacturers test products with irritation and patch tests. In a 2024 study sponsored by Bausch + Lomb, a lash and brow serum, an eye cream and a makeup remover from one brand were assessed in cumulative irritation and repeated insult patch test studies.[2] The study measured tolerability rather than hair growth.

Evidence specific to non-prescription brow serums is very limited. The 2024 sponsored study above evaluated safety and tolerability of one brand's lash and brow serum, not growth.[2] A trial registered as NCT07819721, 'Effects of CosmeRNA Brow Revitalizing Serum on Eyebrow Density and Length', enrolled 26 participants, started in April 2026 and is listed as completed; no results were found.[3]

timeline.event: Latisse introduced as the first FDA-approved eyelash growth drug.[1]
Sponsored safety and tolerability study of a lash and brow serum published.[2]
Brow serum trial NCT07819721 starts and is listed as completed.[3]

card.summary: Cosmetic serums sold to thicken brows; published evidence is limited to a safety test and one small unreported trial.
card.note: Prostaglandin-containing products are drugs and regulated differently; growth data for cosmetic serums are lacking.

quick.overview:
Brow growth serums are topical cosmetics, often with peptides or plant extracts, marketed to make eyebrows look fuller. They are separate from prescription prostaglandin products such as bimatoprost.

Only limited research exists: one sponsored safety study of a lash and brow serum and one small registered trial without located results.
quick.mechanism: Cosmetic serums generally claim to condition hair or support growth through peptides and botanicals; no published study confirms a mechanism for brow growth.
quick.risks: Products near the eye can cause irritation or allergic reactions, which manufacturers screen with patch tests. Prostaglandin-based products have additional documented effects such as eye redness and skin darkening.
